name_en: Bank/police 'safe account' impersonation
summary: A caller or texter posing as the victim's bank fraud team (sometimes the police, National Crime Agency or an internet provider) says the account is compromised and the money must be moved immediately to a new 'safe account', which the criminal controls. Calls often use spoofed numbers, real staff names and data from earlier phishing or breaches, and the victim may be told their own bank is under investigation and coached to lie if the real bank asks why they are moving money.
victim_profile: general public; no specific profile documented (UK Finance says criminals research victims using breach data; Lloyds and Santander case studies involve older customers)
indicators: unexpected call or text saying your account is at risk
instruction to move money to a new or 'safe' account
caller ID shows the bank's real number or a named employee
told your own bank or branch staff are involved in fraud
told to keep the 'investigation' secret or give a false reason for the payment
asked to install remote access software or approve payments
typical_claims: your account has been compromised and money is being taken
move everything to this safe account now or you will lose it
someone at your branch is under investigation, so do not tell them
look up my name on LinkedIn to check I am genuine
if your bank calls, say the payment is genuine
coaching_phrases: tell the bank the payment is genuine if they call
do not tell bank staff the real reason, the bank is under investigation
keep this secret, it is a confidential investigation
give the bank a different reason for moving the money
stay on the line while you make the transfer
say the payment is to your godson for his university fees
choose 'paying friends or family' as the payment type and use a family reference
red_flag_questions: Did someone contact you saying your account was at risk and ask you to move money?
Were you told the new account is a 'safe' or 'holding' account in your name?
Has anyone told you not to trust staff at this bank or to keep this secret?
Were you given a reason to tell us for this payment by someone else?
Is anyone on the phone with you right now?
cues_en: they called from my bank's number
they said my money wasn't safe
the fraud department told me to move it

trend.note: UK Finance 2026 report: police/bank staff impersonation 2025 losses £55.5m (-18%) and 6,016 cases (-23%), lowest ever; but Lloyds (Aug 2026) reports bank and police impersonation up 18% in Q2 2026 year on year.

official_truth: Your bank or the police will never ask you to move money to a 'safe account' to protect it.
advice: Hang up and call your bank on the number on your card or 159 (UK), ideally from a different phone
Never move money to protect it, whatever the caller ID shows
Tell your bank the real reason for any payment, and that someone asked you to lie
Never install remote access apps for an unsolicited caller
applicability_note: The victim initiates a large transfer to a new payee under live phone coaching; a Ruko hold plus call-back can break the spell and surface the 'safe account' story.

name_en: Courier fraud (fake police/bank sends a courier for cash, cards or gold)
summary: A caller posing as a police officer or bank employee claims a card has been used fraudulently or that bank staff or a jeweller are corrupt, and enlists the victim in an 'investigation'. The victim is told to withdraw cash, buy gold, jewellery or watches, or hand over their card and PIN, which a courier then collects from their home; contact can continue for days or weeks with repeat collections.
victim_profile: Older people: City of London Police say those aged 70+ are the majority of victims and 76-96 year olds about 62% of reports; London and surrounding counties about 65% of victims (2025). In Singapore GOIS cash/gold handovers, 40.8% of victims were 65+ (1H 2026).
indicators: large or repeated cash withdrawals by an older customer
unusual purchases of gold, jewellery or luxury watches
customer says police or bank asked for help with an investigation
courier or taxi arranged to collect cash, card or PIN from home
customer told not to speak to branch staff or family
caller asked customer to read or key in their PIN
typical_claims: we have arrested someone using your card
staff at your branch are taking money from accounts and we need evidence
withdraw the cash so we can check it for fingerprints, it will be returned
a courier will collect your card so you do not have to come in
buy gold from this jeweller to help our undercover operation
coaching_phrases: do not discuss this with anyone, including your bank
lie to the bank about why you are withdrawing the money
ignore or get around the bank's security checks
do not contact your bank as it could cause issues with the investigation
write your PIN down and put it in a separate envelope for the courier
red_flag_questions: Has anyone asked you to withdraw cash or buy gold or jewellery to help an investigation?
Is someone coming to your home to collect money, a card or valuables?
Did the caller say staff at this bank are involved?
Were you asked to tell us a particular reason for this withdrawal?
Did you call back on the same landline straight after they rang?
cues_en: put your pin in an envelope
they said it will be returned

trend.note: City of London Police (15 June 2026): reports up from 1,721 in 2024 to 1,891 in 2025; losses from £19.5m to over £21m; gold/jewellery variant growing in 2025.

official_truth: Your bank or the police will never send a courier to your home to collect bank cards, cash or valuables such as jewellery.
advice: Hang up, wait five minutes or use a different phone, then call your bank on 159 or the number on your card
Never hand cash, cards, PINs or valuables to anyone who comes to collect them
Do not trust caller ID; report scam calls by texting 'Call' and the number to 7726
Report to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040
applicability_note: Ruko can hold a large cash withdrawal or a card purchase at a jeweller and call the customer, but card-and-PIN handovers bypass any payment the victim initiates.

name_en: Tax/benefits authority impersonation (HMRC, IRS, SSA, ATO)
summary: A caller, text or email claims to be from the tax or benefits authority (HMRC, IRS, Social Security Administration, ATO) and says the victim owes tax, has a suspended Social Security number or faces arrest, deportation or prosecution unless they pay immediately. A refund variant lures victims to phishing pages. Payment is demanded by bank transfer, gift cards, wire, crypto or payment app, and victims are often told not to tell their bank the real reason.
victim_profile: general public; no specific profile documented (one ombudsman case involved a 63-year-old who had recently stopped working)
indicators: threat of arrest, prison, deportation or licence loss over tax
demand to pay the same day
caller ID matches the agency's real number
payment to a personal account, gift cards, crypto or payment app
told not to tell the bank the payment is for tax
unsolicited text or email about a tax refund with a link
typical_claims: you owe unpaid tax from an audit and must pay today
a warrant has been issued and police will come to your house
your Social Security number has been suspended
you are due a tax refund, click to claim
you must declare your crypto holdings immediately
coaching_phrases: tell the bank the money is for a holiday on a prepaid travel card
do not tell the bank you owe tax or it will close your account
stay on the phone while you are in the branch
keep quiet and do not interrupt while the caller reads out the charges
red_flag_questions: Has someone from a tax or government office asked you to pay them today?
Were you threatened with arrest or court if you did not pay?
Who told you what to tell us about this payment?
Did you receive a letter about this debt before the call?
Are you being asked to pay by gift card, crypto or a transfer to a personal account?
cues_en: they called from the hmrc number

first_seen.value: by 2018 (FOS case of HMRC impersonation call, September 2018)

trend.note: FTC (June 2026): US government impersonator losses about $920 million in 2025, up from $789 million in 2024. Lloyds (Aug 2026): HMRC impersonation cases up 63% year on year (Jul 2025-Jun 2026). UK Finance 'impersonation: other' (incl. tax/fines) fell 1% to £36.9m in 2025.

official_truth: Government agencies will never threaten you with arrest or demand payment by wire, gift card, cryptocurrency or payment app over an unexpected call, text or email.
advice: Hang up and contact the agency on the number from its official website
Never pay a tax demand by gift card, crypto, wire or payment app
Forward HMRC scam texts to 60599 (UK) or ATO scams to ReportScams@ato.gov.au (AU)
Tell your bank the real reason for any payment
applicability_note: The victim pushes a transfer under threat and with a coached cover story; a Ruko call that asks who told them what to say directly targets the documented behaviour.

name_en: 'Hi Mum' / family member new-number message
summary: A message, usually on WhatsApp or SMS, from an unknown number claims to be the victim's child, parent or friend who has lost or broken their phone. After some chat, the impersonator asks for an urgent payment for a bill, contractor or new phone because they 'cannot access online banking', often to an account in another name, and may ask for further transfers. Phone-call variants use fake lawyers or police, or AI-cloned voices, and ask the victim to keep it secret.
victim_profile: Scamwatch (2022): 82% of Australian family impersonation reports were from people over 55, accounting for 95% of losses, and over two-thirds from women over 55. SPF (1H 2026): social media impersonation victims mostly aged 50-64 (35.5%).
indicators: message from an unknown number claiming to be a child or relative
story of a lost, broken or new phone
urgent request to pay a bill or invoice for them
payee name does not match the family member
reluctance to take a voice call
request to keep it between you
typical_claims: hi mum, this is my new number, my phone broke
can you pay this bill for me, my banking app is locked on the new phone
I'll pay you back tomorrow
it's urgent, it has to go today
please don't tell dad
coaching_phrases: keep this secret, do not check with other family members
you are the only one who can help, act now
red_flag_questions: Is this payment for a family member who contacted you from a new number?
Have you spoken to them by voice on the number you already had saved?
Whose name is on the account you are paying?
Were you asked to keep this from other family members?
cues_en: can you do me a favour
my son messaged from a new number
it's not my account it's my friend's

first_seen.value: by 2022 (Scamwatch reported a spike in June-July 2022)

trend.note: Latest official figures found are dated: Scamwatch reported $2.6 million lost in the first seven months of 2022. SPF reports the compromised-WhatsApp variant at 391 cases (66.6% of social media impersonation scams) in 1H 2026, with that category's cases up 47.9%.

official_truth: If someone claims to be your child or relative from a new number, call them on the number already stored in your phone before sending any money.
advice: Call the relative on their old saved number or use another contact method
Ask a personal question a scammer could not answer
Never pay a 'family' bill into an account in someone else's name without voice confirmation
Report to your bank immediately if you have paid
applicability_note: The victim makes a voluntary transfer to a new payee; a Ruko call asking whether they have spoken to the relative on the old number usually breaks it.

name_en: Invoice / mandate redirection (payment diversion, BEC)
summary: A criminal who has compromised or spoofed the email of a supplier, solicitor, conveyancer, builder or title company tells the payer that bank details have changed, or sends a genuine-looking invoice with new payee details, so a payment the victim intended for a legitimate payee goes to the criminal's account. It hits both businesses (supplier invoices) and consumers (house deposits, tradespeople).
victim_profile: Businesses and their finance staff, and consumers paying solicitors, conveyancers or tradespeople; UK Finance: 68% of 2025 invoice and mandate losses were on non-personal (business) accounts. IC3 cases include home buyers closing on property.
indicators: email saying supplier or solicitor bank details have changed
invoice with new payee account just before a large payment
sender address slightly different from the usual one
urgency to pay a house deposit or completion funds today
payee name on the new account does not match the business
first payment ever to this account for a known supplier
typical_claims: please note our bank details have changed, use the account below
here are the wire instructions for your closing
completion funds must reach us today
attached is the updated invoice
red_flag_questions: Is this payment to someone you have paid before, and has their account changed?
How were you told about the new bank details?
Have you called the supplier or solicitor on a number you already had to confirm?
Is this a house deposit or completion payment?

trend.note: UK Finance: invoice & mandate 2025 losses £41.3m (-4%), 2,305 cases (-2%), lowest ever. IC3 2025: BEC losses $3.05 billion (second-largest cyber-enabled fraud). NASC 2025: payment re-direction $166.8m (second by loss in Australia). SPF 1H 2026: BEC losses up 193.1% to S$57.3m.

official_truth: Always verify any change to a payee's bank details by calling them on a number you have sourced independently, never one in the email.
advice: Call the supplier or solicitor on a known number before paying new details
Check the sender address letter by letter
Use Confirmation of Payee or name checks where available
Report to your bank immediately so the receiving account can be frozen
applicability_note: The victim initiates a transfer to a new payee; a Ruko hold that asks whether the new details were verified by phone fits this exactly, though the victim is unaware of the scam so cues come from the payment, not the story.

name_en: CEO / boss impersonation (urgent payment or gift cards)
summary: A fraudster impersonates the CEO, a senior executive or the victim's supervisor, usually by compromising or spoofing their email, and tells a finance team member to make an urgent payment to a new account or change payment details. A common variant asks an employee to move to WhatsApp and buy gift cards (e.g. for staff incentives or client gifts), then send the redemption codes.
victim_profile: Mostly businesses, especially staff responsible for making payments (UK Finance; SPF). Low volume but high value: UK Finance says CEO fraud has the highest average loss of the eight APP types (just over £28,000 per case in 2025).
indicators: urgent payment request from a senior executive by email or chat
instruction to bypass normal approval or keep it confidential
request to switch to a personal WhatsApp number
request to buy gift cards for 'staff incentives' or 'client gifts'
new payee account for a request supposedly from the boss
sender address or display name slightly off
typical_claims: I need you to make an urgent payment today, I'm in a meeting
can you send me your mobile number, let's continue on WhatsApp
buy some gift cards for client gifts and send me the codes
please process this to the new account before cut-off
coaching_phrases: continue the conversation on your personal WhatsApp
buy the gift cards in person, scratch them and send me the redemption codes
red_flag_questions: Did this request come from a senior person by email or chat rather than through your usual approval process?
Have you confirmed it with them by calling a number you already have?
Were you asked to buy gift cards or keep the request confidential?
Is the payee new to your business?

trend.note: UK Finance: CEO fraud 2025 losses £5.6m (-53%) and 197 cases (-29%), the least common APP type. SPF reports wider BEC losses up 193.1% in 1H 2026.

official_truth: Always verify sudden payment instructions or gift card requests from a boss through a separate, known contact before acting.
advice: Call the executive on a known number before any urgent or unusual payment
Never buy gift cards for work on an email or chat request
Follow dual-approval rules even under time pressure
Report spoofed or compromised emails to IT and the bank
applicability_note: Business bank transfers can be held and verified by call, but the gift-card variant moves money at a retail counter outside Ruko's reach.

name_en: Tech support / refund-overpayment scam (remote access)
summary: A fake security pop-up, renewal notice (Geek Squad, McAfee, Norton), Amazon/Microsoft/bank message or cold call leads the victim to a fake technician or refund agent, who gets them to install remote access software (AnyDesk, UltraViewer, ConnectWise). The scammer then either moves money out while the victim is logged in to banking, or stages a fake 'refund', claims too much was paid and pressures the victim to send back the 'overpayment' by transfer, gift cards, crypto or cash. The story often escalates to a fake bank or government agent telling the victim to move savings to 'protect' them.
victim_profile: Older adults are prominent: FTC (2025) reports older adults losing $10,000+ to these impersonators quadrupled 2020-2024; IC3 2025 lists tech support/ATO as the top crime type in elder-fraud recovery incidents.
indicators: pop-up or message telling the customer to call a support number
remote access app installed during a call
customer logs into banking while a 'technician' is connected
claim that a refund was overpaid and must be sent back
request to pay a company or 'refund' via gift cards, crypto or Bitcoin ATM
hand-off from tech support to a 'bank' or 'government' agent
typical_claims: your computer has been hacked, call this number now
your subscription will auto-renew for hundreds of dollars unless you cancel
we refunded you too much by mistake, please send the difference back
install this app so we can fix the firewall
your bank account is compromised, we will transfer you to the fraud team
coaching_phrases: stay on the phone and do not talk to anyone else
log into your bank so we can process the refund
approve the transaction on your token or app when it pops up
red_flag_questions: Is anyone connected to your computer or phone right now, for example through AnyDesk?
Did a pop-up or message ask you to call a support number?
Are you sending money back because of a refund or overpayment?
Did someone ask you to approve a transaction you did not set up yourself?
cues_en: they took control of my screen

trend.note: IC3 2025: tech support losses $2.13 billion (third-largest cyber-enabled fraud), 47,794 complaints. NASC 2025: remote access scams $69.9m (fifth by loss in Australia). FTC: older-adult $10K+ impersonation reports rose from 1,790 (2020) to 8,269 (2024).

official_truth: Real security warnings never ask you to call a phone number, and tech companies do not contact you to report a problem with your computer.
advice: Never install remote access apps for an unsolicited caller or pop-up
Never send back a 'refund overpayment'; check your balance yourself in your banking app
Hang up and call the company or bank on a number you know
If someone had remote access, disconnect and contact your bank immediately
applicability_note: The 'send back the overpayment' and 'protect your money' transfers are victim-initiated and holdable; transfers the scammer makes via remote access look customer-initiated, so a Ruko call is still valuable but the victim may be mid-session with the scammer.

name_en: Romance scam (online partner asks for money)
summary: A fraudster with a fake profile on a dating site or social media builds an intense online relationship over weeks or months, avoids video calls and meetings, then asks for money for a crisis (visa, medical bills, flight tickets, stuck customs package, business or oil-rig problems) or steers the victim into a fake investment. Requests repeat and grow, and victims are often asked to keep the relationship secret and become isolated from family.
victim_profile: general public; Report Fraud notes victims are isolated from family and friends and for almost a third the fraud lasts over a year; no age profile stated in the sources opened
indicators: repeated payments to a person the customer has never met
payee abroad or a third party 'agent'
story of visa, medical, customs or travel costs
relationship began online and moved to WhatsApp/Telegram
customer reluctant to discuss the payee or told to keep it secret
escalating amounts over weeks or months
typical_claims: I'm stuck abroad and need money for the visa
my package is held at customs, can you pay the fee
I'm on an oil rig and can't access my accounts
I'll pay you back as soon as I get home
let me show you how I invest in crypto
coaching_phrases: don't tell anyone about us
keep this between us, your family won't understand
red_flag_questions: Have you met the person you are paying face to face?
Did you meet them online, and have they ever done a live video call?
Is this one of several payments to help them with a problem?
Has anyone asked you not to tell family or the bank about this relationship?

trend.note: UK Finance: romance 2025 losses £39.2m (+23%), 6,335 cases (+22%), fifth consecutive annual case increase, 9.7 payments per scam on average. IC3 2025: confidence/romance $929m. NASC 2025: romance $139.9m (third by loss). SPF 1H 2026: internet love 373 cases, S$8.4M (down).

official_truth: If someone you have only met online asks for money, however sad or urgent the story, it is a scam; never send it.
advice: Never send money, gift cards or crypto to someone you have not met in person
Reverse-image search their profile photos
Talk to a friend or family member before paying
Report the profile to the platform and tell your bank
applicability_note: Victim-initiated, repeated transfers; Ruko's call may meet resistance because the victim believes the relationship, so questions about meeting in person work better than accusations.

name_en: Pig butchering / fake crypto or trading platform investment
summary: Scammers make contact through a wrong-number text, dating app, social media ad or 'investment learning' WhatsApp/Telegram group with fake mentors and members, build trust, then direct the victim to a fake crypto or trading app that shows growing profits. Victims deposit progressively larger sums (bank transfer to 'agents', crypto, or even cash handed to couriers) and when they try to withdraw are hit with 'taxes' or 'fees' before the scammers disappear. Many operations run from Southeast Asian scam compounds using trafficked workers.
victim_profile: general public; IC3 2025 reports crypto investment fraud complainants aged 60+ (13,685 complaints) lost $2.76 billion, the most of any age group; SPF says investment victims are reached via online acquaintances, ads, searches and chat groups.
indicators: first-time transfers to a crypto exchange or to individuals described as 'agents'
customer mentions a mentor, trading group or app showing big profits
escalating deposits after small early withdrawals
request to pay 'tax' or 'fees' before withdrawing profits
contact began with a wrong-number text, dating match or social ad
large cash withdrawal said to be for an investment
typical_claims: join our free investment learning community
our mentor's stock picks made 30% this week
you need to deposit more to reach VIP level
pay the withdrawal tax first and your profits will be released
I made a fortune trading crypto, let me teach you
coaching_phrases: tell the bank the money is for home renovation
the bank will try to stop you, give them a different reason
use the cover story if the branch asks why you are withdrawing cash
red_flag_questions: Is this payment for an investment or trading app someone introduced you to online?
Have you been able to withdraw your money, or were you asked to pay fees or tax first?
Did someone in a chat group or a new online friend recommend this?
Has anyone suggested what you should tell us about this payment?

trend.note: IC3 2025: crypto investment fraud $7.2 billion, the largest US loss source; FTC 2025: investment scams over $7.9 billion, about half of all reported losses; UK Finance 2025: investment scam losses £221.5m (+40%), record high; NASC 2025: investment $837.7m (top by loss); SPF 1H 2026: investment top by loss at S$169.8M (-5.1%).

official_truth: If you were contacted unexpectedly, pressured to invest quickly and promised unrealistic returns, it is almost certainly a scam; check the firm on the regulator's register before paying.
advice: Check the firm on the FCA register (UK) or ASIC (AU) before investing
Never pay 'tax' or 'fees' to unlock withdrawals
Do not invest on advice from online acquaintances or chat-group mentors
Tell your bank the real purpose of any transfer
applicability_note: Deposits are victim-initiated bank transfers or cash withdrawals; UK Finance notes victims often ignore payment warnings, so a live voice call that asks about withdrawals and fees is the strongest lever.

name_en: Purchase scam (fake seller: goods, vehicles, pets, tickets, holiday lets)
summary: A fake seller on a marketplace, social media or a cloned website advertises an item or service below market price (phones, cars, pets, concert tickets, collectibles, holiday rentals) and persuades the buyer to pay by bank transfer or cash rather than the platform's protected payment, sometimes as a 'deposit' or pre-order with delivery promised weeks or months later. After payment the seller disappears; the reverse variant targets sellers with fake proof-of-payment screenshots.
victim_profile: Broad and mostly lower-value: UK Finance says 71% of 2025 APP cases were purchase scams with an average loss of £671; SPF says e-commerce victims were mostly aged 30-49 (41.3%) and contacted on Carousell and Telegram.
indicators: payment by bank transfer to an individual for an item found on a marketplace or social media
price well below market value
seller insists on paying off-platform or refuses card/escrow
deposit or pre-order for a car, pet, tickets or holiday let not yet seen
payee name differs from the seller's name
urgency because 'other buyers are interested'
typical_claims: lots of people want it, pay a deposit now to secure it
pay by bank transfer, the platform's payment doesn't work for me
I'll courier it to you as soon as payment clears
pre-order now, delivery in a few months
I've already sent payment, here's the screenshot
coaching_phrases: pay by bank transfer instead of the platform's secure payment option
pay in cash or by money transfer service
red_flag_questions: Is this payment for something you found online and have not seen in person?
Did the seller ask you to pay by bank transfer rather than through the website's checkout?
Does the account name match the seller you have been talking to?
Is this a deposit for a car, pet, tickets or a holiday rental?
cues_en: too good to be true price

trend.note: UK Finance 2025: purchase scam losses £118.1m (+20%) and 175,809 cases (+5%), highest ever; advance-fee rise driven by deposits for vehicles and holiday rentals that do not exist. SPF 1H 2026: e-commerce scams 3,865 cases (+19.3%), Pokemon card pre-order cases up 116.8%.

official_truth: Be extra cautious if a seller or holiday host asks you to pay by bank transfer or cash; pay by credit card or the platform's protected checkout instead.
advice: Pay by credit card or the platform's own payment system, never off-platform transfer
See vehicles and pets in person before paying any deposit
Check holiday companies for ABTA/ATOL membership
Check the payee name matches the seller
applicability_note: Victim-initiated transfer to a new individual payee; individually small, so Ruko should weight new-payee plus marketplace cues rather than amount alone.

name_en: Advance fee: inheritance, lottery, customs-held goods
summary: The victim is told by email, letter, social media or phone that they are owed a large sum (an inheritance from someone with their surname, an overseas lottery win, a rebate, or gold or jewellery held at customs) and must first pay taxes, legal, banking or release fees. Each payment triggers a new fee with an excuse why it cannot come out of the windfall, and fraudsters stress secrecy and urgency.
victim_profile: general public; no specific profile documented
indicators: payment of 'fees' or 'taxes' to release an inheritance, prize or parcel
payee overseas or a 'lawyer' or 'agent' account
series of escalating fee payments
customer says they will receive a much larger sum soon
told to keep the windfall secret
no lottery was entered
typical_claims: a relative with your surname died and left millions
you have won an international lottery, pay the processing fee
your gold is held at customs, pay clearance to release it
just one more tax payment and the funds will be released
we can't deduct the fee from the inheritance, it must be paid upfront
coaching_phrases: keep this deal secret and do not tell anyone
act quickly before the money goes to the government
think how close you are and how much you have already paid
red_flag_questions: Are you paying a fee to receive an inheritance, prize, refund or parcel?
Is this the first fee or one of several?
Did you enter the lottery or know the person who left the money?
Has anyone asked you to keep this to yourself?

first_seen.value: unknown (Report Fraud links the 419 name to a Nigerian criminal code article)

trend.note: UK Finance 2025: advance fee scam losses £58.4m (+65%), 24,080 cases (+38%), highest loss total ever; growth driven by fake deposits for vehicles and holiday rentals as well as inheritance/lottery/customs claims.

official_truth: There is no free money: genuine lotteries, lawyers and government departments never ask you to pay a fee upfront to release winnings, an inheritance or a rebate.
advice: Never pay a fee to receive money you were not expecting
Stop contact and verify any 'lawyer' or 'official' independently
Check with your bank or a trusted person before paying
Never share bank details to 'receive' funds
applicability_note: Repeated victim-initiated fee payments, often international; Ruko can ask what the payment releases and whether earlier fees were paid.

name_en: Parcel redelivery / unpaid toll text (smishing)
summary: A text, iMessage or email posing as a postal or courier company (the FTC cites USPS, UPS and FedEx; UK texts use brands such as Royal Mail or Evri) or a toll agency says a parcel could not be delivered or a toll is unpaid and asks for a small fee via a link. The fake site harvests card details, online banking credentials and one-time passcodes; criminals then add the card to Apple Pay or Google Pay, log in from a new device, or follow up with a fake bank 'fraud team' call that leads into a safe account scam.
victim_profile: general public; SPF (1H 2026) says phishing victims were mostly aged 30-49 (40.8%)
indicators: text about a failed delivery or unpaid toll with a link
small redelivery or toll fee requested
sender is a random email address or overseas number
OTP or token approval requested right after entering card details
new device or digital wallet added to the card shortly after
follow-up call from 'the bank' about suspicious activity
typical_claims: your parcel could not be delivered due to an invalid address
pay a small redelivery fee to reschedule
you have an outstanding toll balance, pay now to avoid penalties
enter the code we sent to confirm your payment
red_flag_questions: Did you recently enter card details after a text about a parcel or toll?
Did you share a one-time code or approve something in your banking app afterwards?
Has anyone called you since, claiming to be from the bank?
Do you recognise this new device or wallet on your card?

trend.note: SPF 1H 2026: phishing scams 3,104 cases (down from 3,772) with an ongoing iMessage courier-redelivery trend; NASC 2025: phishing $97.6m (fourth by loss) and the most reported Scamwatch scam (65,361 reports), while text-message scam reports fell from 77,365 to 29,058.

official_truth: Do not click links in unexpected delivery or toll texts; check directly with the courier or toll agency using its official website or app.
advice: Never click links in unexpected delivery or toll texts
Never share one-time passcodes or approve token requests you did not start
Forward scam texts to 7726 (UK/US)
If you entered card details, call your bank to block the card
applicability_note: Money mostly leaves through stolen card details or wallet provisioning rather than a victim transfer, so Ruko helps mainly when the harvested data feeds a follow-up safe-account call.

name_en: Gift card payment demand
summary: Across many storylines (government agency, tech support, family emergency, prize, utility shut-off, romance, or a 'boss' needing gifts for clients), the scammer insists the victim pays by buying gift cards such as Google Play, Apple, Amazon or Razer Gold and reading out or photographing the card numbers and PINs. Victims are kept on the phone and told to spread purchases across several stores so staff do not get suspicious.
victim_profile: general public; no specific profile documented
indicators: large or repeated gift card purchases, often at several stores
customer on the phone while buying cards
request to photograph or read out card numbers and PINs
story of paying a government fee, utility bill, tech fix or boss's request with gift cards
cash withdrawal immediately followed by gift card purchases
typical_claims: pay your fine with Google Play cards to avoid arrest
buy Apple gift cards and read me the numbers
scratch the back and send me a photo of the code
buy them at different shops so it doesn't look odd
I need gift cards for client gifts, I'll reimburse you
coaching_phrases: buy the cards at several different stores so the cashier does not get suspicious
stay on the phone while you buy and load the cards
send the card number and PIN or a photo of the back
red_flag_questions: Has someone asked you to pay them with gift cards?
Are you on the phone with anyone while buying these?
Have you been asked to send photos or numbers from the back of the cards?
Who will you be giving these cards to?
cues_en: send a photo of the card

trend.note: FTC Data Book 2024: gift card or reload card cited in 41,120 fraud reports with $212M lost in 2024 (versus $2,089M by bank transfer), so it is frequent but lower-value; SPF 1H 2026 highlights Razer Gold cards in a BEC/CEO variant.

official_truth: No real business or government agency will ever tell you to buy a gift card to pay them.
advice: Never pay anyone with gift cards on request
Hang up if a caller tells you to buy or load cards while on the phone
Never share card numbers, PINs or photos of cards
If you already paid, contact the card issuer immediately and keep the receipt
applicability_note: Ruko can hold the card purchase or the cash withdrawal that funds it and call the customer, but card codes once read out cannot be recalled.

name_en: Recovery room / fund recovery scam
summary: People who have already lost money (often to investment or crypto scams) are contacted by, or find online ads for, fake law firms, 'asset recovery' companies, government agencies or police who say they can trace and recover the lost funds. Victims are asked for an upfront fee, a percentage, a 'tax', personal and bank details, or remote access, and then for more payments to continue the 'investigation'; nothing is recovered.
victim_profile: Previous scam victims, whose details are traded on 'sucker lists' (FTC). IC3 2025: 60+ complainants reported $540.5m of recovery-scam losses, the most of any age group.
indicators: customer was recently scammed and is now paying a 'recovery' firm or lawyer
fee, percentage or tax demanded before funds are returned
caller claims to be police, a regulator or a government body offering to recover money
request for remote access or bank details to 'deposit' a refund
repeat payments to fund an 'investigation'
recovery service found via online ad promising to trace crypto
typical_claims: we have traced your stolen crypto and can return it
we are a law firm working with the authorities on your case
pay the release fee and your funds will be returned within days
your refund is ready, we just need your bank details
the investigation needs another payment to continue
red_flag_questions: Have you lost money to a scam before, and is this payment to get it back?
Who contacted you offering to recover the money?
Are you being asked to pay a fee, tax or percentage before receiving anything?
Has anyone asked to access your computer or phone remotely?
cues_en: we can get your money back
other victims got their money back

trend.note: IC3 2025 notes an increase in complaints reporting impersonation of government officials and recovery firms; recovery scams 10,516 complaints and $1.4 billion in losses (losses may include earlier scams).

official_truth: Real government agencies never charge a fee or ask for your bank details to help you get scam losses back, and no one can promise you will recover your money.
advice: Never pay anyone who offers to recover scam losses for a fee
Work only with your own bank and the police on recovery
Never give remote access or bank details to a recovery caller
Report recovery offers to the police or national reporting service
applicability_note: Victim-initiated fee payments by people already flagged as scam victims, which makes them a strong candidate for a Ruko hold and call.

name_en: Fake friend call ('guess who') loan request
summary: A caller from an unknown number (phone or WhatsApp) asks the victim to guess who is calling, poses as an acquaintance, and says they lost their phone and changed number. After establishing rapport, the 'friend' asks for an urgent loan, for example to pay renovation contractors, new-business costs or suppliers, which the victim sends by PayNow to a bank account belonging to an unknown person; some callers also push links or app installs.
victim_profile: general public; no specific profile documented on the ScamShield page
indicators: call from an unknown number that starts with 'guess who I am'
friend claims a lost phone and new number
urgent loan request for renovation, business opening or supplier payment
payee is a third party, not the friend
request to click a link or install an app
typical_claims: guess who this is
I lost my phone, this is my new number
I need to pay my renovation contractor, can you lend me some money
I'm opening a new business and need to pay a vendor
click this link / install this app to help me
red_flag_questions: Did the person ask you to guess who was calling?
Have you called them back on the number you had saved before?
Is the money going to an account in their own name?
What is the loan for, and when did they first contact you from this number?
cues_en: it's me, don't you recognise my voice

trend.note: SPF Mid-Year Brief 2026: fake friend call scams fell to 353 cases and S$818K in 1H 2026 from 1,052 cases and S$3.0M in 1H 2025; SPF also reported significant falls for full-year 2025.

official_truth: Verify a caller who claims to be a friend by calling their last known number before transferring any money.
advice: Call the friend on their old saved number or check via social media
Never transfer money to a third-party account on a phone request
Do not click links or install apps sent by the caller
Call your bank and make a police report if you paid
applicability_note: Victim-initiated PayNow/bank transfer to an unknown individual; a Ruko call asking whether they phoned the friend's old number is decisive.

name_en: Government officials impersonation scam (Singapore GOIS, incl. foreign police)
summary: A call that starts as a bank, telco or financial-institution representative (e.g. about a suspicious card transaction, new phone line or unpaid bill) is 'transferred' to someone posing as an SPF, MAS or MinLaw officer, or in a smaller variant an ICA officer, airline or telco then foreign law enforcement, who accuses the victim of money laundering or other crimes. Victims are told to move money to a government 'safety account', make ATM cash deposits, hand cash, gold or luxury watches to 'officers', or show ID and bank cards on WhatsApp video, sometimes for 'investigation or bail'.
victim_profile: Mostly older people: SPF says 40.8% of GOIS victims in 1H 2026 were aged 65 and above; phone calls and WhatsApp were the main channels.
indicators: customer says police, MAS or MinLaw are investigating them
call began as a bank or telco query and was transferred to an 'officer'
transfer to a new account described as a government or safety account
large ATM cash deposits or cash/gold/watch purchases
customer on a WhatsApp video call with an 'officer'
mention of money laundering, bail or foreign police
typical_claims: there is a suspicious transaction on your credit card, let me transfer you to the police
your identity was used for money laundering
transfer your savings to this safety account while we investigate
hand the cash and gold to our officer for investigation
you need to pay bail or a guarantee to the foreign police
coaching_phrases: transfer your money to the government-designated safety account
hand over cash, gold or valuables to the officer who will meet you
show your identity card and bank cards on the video call
deposit the cash at an ATM into the account we give you
red_flag_questions: Has anyone claiming to be from the police, MAS or MinLaw contacted you about an investigation?
Was your call transferred from a bank or telco to an officer?
Have you been asked to move money to a 'safety account' or hand cash or valuables to someone?
Are you on a video call with anyone right now?
cues_en: new phone line in your name
show your bank card on video

trend.note: SPF Mid-Year Brief 2026: GOIS 1,363 cases and S$90.8M in 1H 2026 (from 1,772 and S$132.9M in 1H 2025, losses -31.7%) yet still second-highest by loss; continuing trend of ATM cash deposits and cash/valuables handovers; at least 30 VoIP-based reports.

official_truth: Government officials will never ask you to transfer money, disclose bank log-in details or transfer your call to the Police over a phone call.
advice: Hang up and call the ScamShield Helpline 1799 to check
Never transfer money or hand valuables to anyone claiming to be an officer
Check government SMSes come from the gov.sg sender ID
Consider Money Lock on part of your savings
applicability_note: Victim-initiated transfers and cash withdrawals under threat; a Ruko call can deliver the 'officials never ask you to transfer money' line, though victims may be kept on a live video call.

name_en: Task-based job scam (pay to unlock commissions)
summary: An unsolicited text or WhatsApp/Telegram message, or a social media ad, offers easy remote work such as liking videos, rating products, apps or restaurants, or 'boosting' orders for a commission. After small early payouts, the victim is told to deposit their own money (often crypto or transfers to individuals) to unlock the next set of tasks, complete 'double tasks' or withdraw earnings, with group chats of fake members pushing them on; deposits grow until the victim cannot withdraw anything.
victim_profile: SPF 1H 2026: job scam victims mostly aged 30-49 (38.6%), contacted mainly on WhatsApp and Facebook.
indicators: recent unsolicited job offer by text or WhatsApp
payments to individuals or crypto exchange described as 'top-ups' for tasks
customer mentions commissions for liking, rating or reviewing
escalating deposits after small payouts
told to pay to withdraw earnings
no interview or contract
typical_claims: earn money from home by liking videos or rating products
complete a set of 40 tasks to get your commission
you've got a double task with a bigger commission, top up to complete it
deposit more to withdraw your earnings
our team members earned thousands this week
red_flag_questions: Is this payment connected to an online job or tasks you were offered?
Did you have to pay or top up money to continue working or withdraw earnings?
How did the recruiter first contact you?
Have you been able to withdraw what you earned?

trend.note: FTC: task-scam reports rose from about 5,000 in all of 2023 to about 20,000 in 1H 2024 (rising then). SPF 1H 2026: job scams fell 17.3% to 2,247 cases and 45.5% to about S$34.9M.

official_truth: Never pay anyone to get paid; a genuine job will not ask you to top up money to complete tasks or withdraw earnings.
advice: Ignore unsolicited job messages offering pay for liking or rating
Never deposit money or crypto to unlock tasks or withdraw earnings
Never move money or packages for an 'employer'
Report the recruiter account to the platform
applicability_note: Victim-initiated top-up transfers to individuals or exchanges; Ruko should ask whether they are paying to get paid.

name_en: Bitcoin/crypto ATM cash deposit ('safety locker')
summary: Usually the cash-out stage of a government, business (bank, Amazon) or tech-support impersonation scam: the victim is told their money is at risk or tied to a crime and must be 'protected' or a problem fixed. They are instructed to withdraw cash from their bank, go to a specific Bitcoin ATM (sometimes described as a 'safety locker') and scan a QR code sent by text, which sends the cash irreversibly to the scammer's crypto wallet, often while kept on the phone.
victim_profile: Older adults: FTC (1H 2024) says people 60+ were over three times as likely to report a Bitcoin ATM loss and accounted for about 71% of losses; IC3 2025 says 60+ lost $257.5m of the $389m reported at crypto ATMs/kiosks.
indicators: large cash withdrawal by an older customer with no clear purpose
customer on the phone during the withdrawal
mention of a Bitcoin ATM, crypto kiosk or QR code
story about protecting money, a hacked account or a government investigation
repeat withdrawals over consecutive days
customer asks how much cash can be taken out today
typical_claims: your bank account has been hacked, move your cash to a safe place
deposit the cash in this Bitcoin machine to protect it
scan the QR code I just texted you
this is a government safety locker
stay on the line until the deposit is done
coaching_phrases: withdraw the cash and go to this specific Bitcoin ATM
scan the QR code we text you
stay on the phone while you do it
red_flag_questions: Are you planning to put this cash into a Bitcoin or crypto machine?
Has someone told you to move your money to protect it?
Is anyone on the phone with you or texting you a QR code?
Who told you to withdraw this cash today?
cues_en: they texted me a code to scan

first_seen.value: by 2020 (FTC tracks Bitcoin ATM losses from 2020)

trend.note: FTC: Bitcoin ATM losses rose nearly tenfold 2020-2023 and topped $65 million in 1H 2024. IC3 2025: crypto ATM/kiosk complaints 13,460 (+23%) and losses $389 million (+58%).

official_truth: No real business or government agency will ever tell you to withdraw cash and deposit it into a Bitcoin ATM to protect your money; anyone who does is a scammer.
advice: Hang up on anyone telling you to move money to protect it
Never deposit cash into a crypto ATM at someone's instruction
Call your bank or the agency on a number you know
Report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov or to IC3
applicability_note: The crypto ATM deposit is cash, but it is funded by a bank withdrawal Ruko can hold and call about; once cash is in hand the bank cannot intervene.

name_en: Sextortion (pay or intimate images are shared)
summary: An unknown or hacked social media account starts a flirtatious chat, quickly moves it to an encrypted messaging app and pressures the victim into sharing intimate images (or fabricates them with AI, or falsely claims to have hacked the victim's device). The offender then threatens to send the images to the victim's contacts unless they pay money or buy gift cards, and demands continue after each payment.
victim_profile: Young people are most affected by count: IC3 2025 received over 75,000 sextortion submissions, with the most from those aged 20-29; the FTC (2023 spotlight) said 18-29 year olds were over six times as likely to report it as people 30 and over.
indicators: distressed customer making urgent payments to an unknown person or overseas account
payment demanded within minutes or hours
recent new online contact who moved chat to a private app
gift card purchases or crypto transfers under threat
repeated escalating demands
typical_claims: pay now or I send these pictures to all your followers
I have your contacts list and your family's names
you have one hour to pay
send gift cards and I will delete everything
I hacked your camera and recorded you
red_flag_questions: Is someone threatening to share images or information unless you pay?
Did you recently meet this person online?
Have you already paid them once?
Would you like us to connect you with police support instead of paying?

trend.note: FTC (Feb 2023): sextortion reports rose more than eightfold since 2019. IC3 2025: more than 75,000 sextortion submissions.

official_truth: Paying does not stop sextortion; once you pay, offenders usually demand more, so stop contact, keep the evidence and report it to police.
advice: Stop all contact and block the offender
Do not pay, or pay nothing more
Keep messages and payment details as evidence
Report to police and to the platform; under-18s can use Report Remove or Take It Down
applicability_note: Payments are victim-initiated under panic; Ruko can hold and call, but the call must be handled sensitively and route the person to support rather than question them.

name_en: Fake loan with upfront fee
summary: Ads on social media or search, or unsolicited SMS/WhatsApp messages, offer fast cash loans approved regardless of credit history. Before the loan is released the applicant must pay an upfront fee (such as 'insurance', processing or a deposit) by bank transfer, PayNow, ATM cash deposit or cash handover, and the lender then disappears without paying out.
victim_profile: general public; no specific profile documented (people seeking fast credit)
indicators: payment to a 'lender' before receiving any loan
loan found via social media ad or unsolicited message
approval despite poor credit with no checks
fee described as insurance, processing or guarantee
payee is an individual's account
typical_claims: your loan is approved, no credit check needed
pay the insurance fee first and the loan will be released
fast cash in 30 minutes
one more processing fee and we will disburse today
red_flag_questions: Are you paying a fee to receive a loan?
How did you find this lender?
Have you checked the lender on the official register?
Have you received any of the loan yet?

trend.note: SPF 1H 2026: loan scams 384 cases and S$2.1M (from 456 and S$3.3M in 1H 2025). FTC Data Book 2024: 'Advance Payments for Credit Services' had 27,557 reports.

official_truth: Never pay an upfront fee as a condition of getting a loan; that is how loan scams work.
advice: Never pay upfront fees for a loan
Check the lender on the FCA register (UK) or Registry of Moneylenders (SG)
Ignore loan ads and unsolicited loan messages
Avoid paying by bank transfer to unknown lenders
applicability_note: Victim-initiated fee transfer to a new payee; Ruko can ask whether the payment is a fee to unlock a loan.

name_en: Money mule recruitment (receive and forward money)
summary: People are recruited, often through job offers, online contacts or romance and investment scams, to let criminals use their bank account, Singpass or SIM card, or to receive money and transfer it on (sometimes keeping a cut). The account holder may not realise they are laundering scam proceeds, but faces account closure and criminal penalties; in Singapore mules face prison, fines and caning.
victim_profile: general public; job seekers are targeted via 'jobs' that involve transferring money or receiving packages (Scamwatch); no age profile documented in sources opened
indicators: incoming payments from unknown people followed quickly by outgoing transfers
customer says an employer or online contact asked them to move money
job role described as payment processing or transferring funds
request to lend bank login, card, Singpass or SIM to someone
outgoing transfers to crypto exchanges right after deposits
typical_claims: the job is just transferring money and receiving packages for us
you'll be paid for moving funds through your account
let us use your bank account or Singpass for a while
send the money on to this account and keep something for yourself
red_flag_questions: Did this money come from someone you know, and why are you sending it on?
Has anyone offered you a job or a cut for moving money through your account?
Has anyone else used your banking app, card or login?
Who asked you to make this transfer?
cues_en: funds came in, send them out

trend.note: SPF 1H 2026: more than 2,900 money mules and scammers investigated and at least 470 charged; caning for scam-related offences introduced 30 December 2025.

official_truth: Never let anyone use your bank account, card, Singpass or SIM card, or move money through your account for someone you do not know and trust; doing so can make you a money mule and a criminal.
advice: Never receive and forward money for a stranger or 'employer'
Never share bank logins, cards, Singpass or SIMs
Report unexpected incoming funds to your bank
Treat any job that involves moving money as a scam
applicability_note: The mule's onward transfer is customer-initiated and can be held; a Ruko call both protects the mule and may surface the upstream victim's payment.
